## Spatial Exposure Construction
Because county boundaries are government-defined, they often do not represent meaningful geographic divisions within an area. As such, the addition of a data center in one county does not guarantee that it will have no impact on nearby areas located in another county. If a resident lives within a few miles of a county boundary and a data center is built on the other side of that boundary, it is likely that, if data centers have an impact at all, they may also affect that resident. We therefore tried to account for this effect in our modeling by creating a spatial exposure measure. 

For each county, we constructed a 50-mile Euclidean buffer around the target county’s boundaries. We selected 50 miles as an intermediate regional scale: it is broad enough to capture cross-county interactions, but narrow enough to avoid defining an entire state or multi-state area as a single local economy. We decided to use a buffer instead of county adjacency for data centers because the physical size of U.S. counties varies substantially, and we did not want data centers on one side of a very large county, potentially trying to describe differences in parts of another county, potentially hundreds of miles away. 

@fig-50-mile-buffer illustrates this process using Multnomah County, Oregon. The orange-shaded areas represent the portions of neighboring counties that fall within Multnomah County’s 50-mile buffer and therefore contribute, in proportion to their overlapping land area, to the nearby data center exposure measure. As shown in the figure, the buffer extends 50 miles outward from every point along the county boundary rather than from a single central point. It therefore follows the county’s irregular shape. Where the county boundary turns at a corner, the 50-mile offsets from adjacent boundary segments meet in a rounded arc rather than in a sharp or jagged point.

```{python}
# Set variables
BUFFER_MILES = 50
BUFFER_METERS = BUFFER_MILES * 1609.344
SQM_PER_SQMI = 2_589_988.110336

gray_fill = "#d9d9d9"
gray_edge = "#9e9e9e"
county_fill = "#2f5d8a"
county_edge = "#17324d"
buffer_fill = "#f4a261"
buffer_edge = "#d97706"
overlap_fill = "#f28e2b"
overlap_edge = "#b45309"

# Create buffer df
geojson_path = data_dir / "county_fips_codes" / "geojson_counties_fips.json"
counties_geo = gpd.read_file(geojson_path)
counties_geo["id"] = counties_geo["id"].replace({"46113": "46102"})
counties_geo = counties_geo[["id", "geometry"]].copy()
counties_geo = counties_geo.rename(columns={"id": "county_id"})
counties_geo["county_id"] = counties_geo["county_id"].astype(str)

counties_final = df_county.merge(counties_geo, on="county_id", how="left")
counties_final = gpd.GeoDataFrame(counties_final, geometry="geometry", crs="EPSG:4326").to_crs(5070)
counties_final["geometry"] = counties_final.geometry.make_valid()

counties_final["geom_area_sqmi"] = counties_final.geometry.area / SQM_PER_SQMI
counties_final["total_area_sqmi"] = counties_final["land_area_sqmi"] + counties_final["water_area_sqmi"]
counties_final["land_share"] = counties_final["land_area_sqmi"] / counties_final["total_area_sqmi"]

# Create mulnomah-specific buffer
multnomah = counties_final[counties_final["county_id"] == "41051"].copy()

buffers = multnomah[["county_id", "geometry"]].copy()
buffers["geometry"] = buffers.geometry.buffer(BUFFER_METERS)
buffers = buffers.rename(columns={"county_id": "target_county_id"})

# Identify counties that intersect Multnomah County's 50-mile buffer
candidate_pairs = gpd.sjoin(
    buffers,
    counties_final[["county_id", "geometry"]],
    how="inner",
    predicate="intersects"
)

candidate_pairs = candidate_pairs.rename(
    columns={"county_id": "neighbor_county_id"}
)

candidate_pairs = candidate_pairs[
    candidate_pairs["target_county_id"] != candidate_pairs["neighbor_county_id"]
].copy()

candidate_pairs = candidate_pairs[
    ["target_county_id", "neighbor_county_id"]
].drop_duplicates()


# Attach the buffer geometry and neighboring county geometry
buffer_geom = buffers.rename(
    columns={"geometry": "buffer_geometry"}
)

neighbor_geom = counties_final[
    ["county_id", "geometry", "land_share", "geom_area_sqmi"]
].rename(
    columns={
        "county_id": "neighbor_county_id",
        "geometry": "neighbor_geometry",
        "land_share": "neighbor_land_share",
        "geom_area_sqmi": "neighbor_geom_area_sqmi"
    }
)

overlap = (
    candidate_pairs
    .merge(buffer_geom, on="target_county_id", how="left")
    .merge(neighbor_geom, on="neighbor_county_id", how="left")
)

buffer_series = gpd.GeoSeries(overlap["buffer_geometry"], crs=counties_final.crs)
neighbor_series = gpd.GeoSeries(overlap["neighbor_geometry"], crs=counties_final.crs)
intersection_geom = buffer_series.intersection(neighbor_series, align=False)

overlap = gpd.GeoDataFrame(overlap, geometry=intersection_geom, crs=counties_final.crs)
overlap = overlap[overlap.geometry.notna() & ~overlap.geometry.is_empty].copy()
```

Since we did not have the exact location of each data center, we estimated nearby data center exposure by assuming an equal distribution of data centers across each county. Each intersecting county’s data center count was weighted by the proportion of its land area contained within the buffer. These weighted values were then summed for each county with an overlap with the buffer. This approach gave a smaller contribution to counties that only marginally overlapped the buffer and a larger contribution to counties with substantial or complete overlap, avoiding the assumption that all nearby counties were equally exposed. The final result of these calculations was a “total nearby data centers” feature that we could use in our modeling, in addition to the in-county data center feature we already had. 

For other economic variables, we also wanted to incorporate information from nearby counties, but felt that the approach used for data centers did not translate well, mostly because economic aggregates cannot be assumed to be evenly distributed across a county in the same way. There is no physical location of an economic descriptor that we are trying to estimate; rather, we are trying to capture general regional trends. Therefore, we decided to use an inverse-distance-weighting approach for our economic variables. Specifically, we calculated weighted averages for rate-based measures where a regional mean was meaningful and weighted sums for count-based measures where aggregate nearby activity was the relevant quantity. Counties closer to the target county’s centroid received a larger weight than more distant counties, and the number of nearby counties included in each calculation was limited to five. Limiting the calculation to the five nearest counties captured a more immediate regional context while reducing the influence of distant counties that are less likely to share economic conditions or infrastructure with the target county.

## Statistical Approach
Our initial statistical assessments revealed that many features across nearly all data sources exhibited extreme right-skew. Because severe skew distorts linear regressions and distance-based machine learning models, we implemented several transformation strategies. First, any skewed features received a logarithmic transformation. For features containing zero values, NumPy's log1p function was used to prevent undefined log-zero errors; otherwise, the standard log function was used. For algorithms such as Principal Component Analysis (PCA), random forests, neural networks, and logistic regression, where some features retained enough skew after logarithmic transformation and standardization to degrade model performance, we initially scaled features using scikit-learn’s StandardScaler however this proved inadequate for extremly skewed features. To fix this, we adopted the Yeo-Johnson power transformation. By applying an optimal power parameter to stabilize variance and minimize skewness across both positive and negative values, this approach successfully mapped feature distributions to an approximately Gaussian space for downstream modeling.

Our dataset exhibited severe class imbalance, as the vast majority of county-year observations contained zero data centers. Left unaddressed, this imbalance caused significant prediction bias and poor performance in our machine learning models. We leveraged built-in class weighting mechanisms (such as class_weight='balanced' in scikit-learn's LogisticRegression) to assign higher penalty weights to errors on the minority class during training. In cases where the balanced weight parameter didn’t improve the model or was unavailable, we applied the Synthetic Minority Oversampling Technique (SMOTE) to generate synthetic instances within the feature space of the minority class, rebalancing the training distribution.
While initial evaluations included classical statistical frameworks like linear and logistic regression, these models yielded limited explanatory power and low statistical significance. Consequently, we adopted Difference-in-Differences (DiD) as our primary analytical framework. This shift was supported by prior literature in the field and the method's ability to isolate treatment effects and support stronger causal inferences regarding data center deployment.

Difference-in-differences models estimate the effect of a treatment on a population over time by comparing treated units against a control group over the same observation window that did not receive the treatment. This framework is particularly well-suited for settings where randomized controlled trials cannot be practically or ethically implemented, as is typical in most empirical economic investigations. Furthermore, DiD designs do not rely on all of the strict statistical assumptions required by standard linear or logistic regression specifications. Instead, the validity of the DiD design primarily depends on the Parallel Trends assumption. This assumption requires that during the pre-intervention period, the treatment and control groups exhibit no statistically significant differences in their outcome trends relative to one another. Under this condition, any statistically significant divergence between the two groups following the intervention can be attributed to the causal impact of the treatment.

Because data centers enter and exit counties at different points in time, we leverage the Callaway and Sant’Anna [@Callaway2021difference] DiD estimator, which accommodates staggered treatment timing across units. We define the treatment as the first year in which a county reaches three or more data centers. We evaluated multiple treatment definitions within the DiD framework, initially defining treatment as a transition from zero data centers to one or more. Ultimately, setting the threshold to a transition from two or fewer data centers in a prior year to three or more in the subsequent year best satisfied our dual mandate of generating the clearest post-treatment trends while satisfying the pre-treatment parallel trends assumption. This higher threshold likely filters out noise introduced by the linear imputation of missing values in the QCEW NAICS 518 dataset, providing a more definitive indicator of substantive year-over-year data center growth. For nearby data centers, we similarly defined treatment as crossing the threshold of 113 data centers within 50 miles (corresponding to approximately the 75th percentile of the distribution). This stronger statistical signal for both in-county and nearby data centers reflects both the more pronounced, detectable economic footprint of larger regional clusters and a reduced sensitivity to underlying imputation artifacts.

The general formulation for the Callaway and Sant’Anna group-time average treatment effect is defined as:
$$\text{ATT}(g, t) = \mathbb{E}[Y_{i,t}(g) - Y_{i,t}(0) \mid G_i = g]$$
Here, $\text{ATT}(g, t)$ represents the group-time average treatment effect for units $i$ that first adopted the treatment in cohort year g. While we apply this model across multiple outcome variables, consider an illustrative model estimating the impact of receiving a third data center on a county's unemployment rate. The parameter is calculated by taking the expected value ($\mathbb{E}$) of the difference between two potential outcomes: $Y_{i,t}(g)$, which represents the unemployment rate observed in county $i$ in year $t$ given that it crossed the treatment threshold in year $g$, and $Y_{i,t}(0)$, which represents the unobserved counterfactual unemployment rate county $i$ would have experienced in year $t$ had it never received the treatment. Because $Y_{i,t}(0)$ cannot be directly observed, it is estimated by adding the average observed change in unemployment across control (never-treated) counties to the baseline value of the treated county. For example, if Multnomah County gains its third data center in 2009 ($g = 2009$) and records an actual unemployment rate of 2.5% ($Y_{\text{Multnomah}, 2009}$), calculating the counterfactual requires its 2008 baseline rate (e.g., 2.4%) and the average change in unemployment among never-treated counties between 2008 and 2009 (e.g., +0.7%). The counterfactual outcome $Y_{\text{Multnomah}, 2009}(0)$ is estimated as $2.4\% + 0.7\% = 3.1\%$. The resulting treatment effect is the difference between the observed value $2.5\%$ and this counterfactual ($3.1\%$), yielding a treatment effect of $-0.6\%$. This calculation is performed for every county treated in cohort $g$, and the resulting individual effects are averaged to produce $\text{ATT}(g, t)$.


## Machine Learning Approach
To account for the fact that counties across the U.S. can have structurally different local economies and thus may react differently to the introduction of data centers, we developed an unsupervised machine learning pipeline using dimensionality reduction and clustering. This segmentation serves two roles across our methodology: it stratifies our Difference-in-Differences (DiD) models across distinct county cohorts, and it establishes the subgroups used to train separate generative models (Variational Autoencoders) for counterfactual simulation.

### K-means Clustering
During exploratory analysis, we used PCA to examine the underlying geometric structure of our dataset. Projecting the data onto the first two principal components revealed distinct structural patterns across county observations. When visualizing these projections, we observed clear spatial separation between counties with and without data centers. Crucially, this separation persisted even when training the PCA model on a feature set that explicitly excluded the data center count. Color-coding the projection by the log-transformed data center count (applied due to extreme right-skew from high-density outlier counties) reinforced this pattern. The underlying feature set cleanly separated counties based on data center presence, suggesting fundamental structural differences in local economic and demographic profiles.

To formalize these subgroupings and test whether different county types respond differently to data center deployment, we implemented k-means clustering. We evaluated various cluster counts using the silhouette score to quantify separation. Across iterations, $k = 2$ consistently yielded the highest silhouette score. Passing the top principal components into the k-means algorithm rather than raw features further improved cluster separation and maximized the overall silhouette score.

Mapping cluster assignments spatially revealed geographic clusters even without spatial coordinates or centroid locations included in the input features. Comparing summary statistics across both groups confirmed that cluster assignment primarily aligned with population density and economic scale. Consequently, we interpreted Cluster 0 as predominantly rural counties and Cluster 1 as urban counties, aligning our empirical grouping with existing literature that stratifies local economic impacts along rural and urban lines.

We used k-means clustering because we suspected that distinct classes of counties would respond differently to an additional data center. Logically, some counties are much larger in terms of population and economic activity, meaning a new data center, even a large one, would have a minimal effect relative to the overall economy. By testing various cluster counts, we found that $k = 2$ provided the best separation.

While our k-means clustering model yielded two distinct groups, the approach introduced trade-offs compared to traditional binary classifications. The primary advantage of multi-feature k-means clustering is that it optimizes mathematical separation across the entire feature space, improving downstream model performance. However, this comes at the cost of interpretability. Because the model ingested a broad set of economic and demographic variables (excluding explicit geographic coordinates and data center counts), the resulting clusters reflected complex, multidimensional similarities beyond a simple rural versus urban split. Running PCA on the full feature set introduced potential data leakage risks relative to downstream targets. To resolve this and improve model transparency, we restricted a second pass of the PCA and k-means pipeline strictly to baseline structural predictors: total population and physical county area.

Mapping and evaluating summary statistics for this refined two-cluster split produced geographic and demographic distributions nearly identical to our initial run. This confirmed that population density and county scale drive the underlying structural separation while significantly boosting model interpretability and preventing feature leakage.

### Conditional Variational Autoencoder Models
We implement a Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) to complement
our Difference-in-Differences (DiD) framework. While DiD provides a quasi-experimental comparison between treated and control counties, the model learns a continuous latent representation of each county's unique socio-economic trajectory. By identifying the specific vector within the model's latent space that corresponds to variations in data center count, we can perturb that direction while holding all other latent features constant. Reconstructing the output from this modified latent representation creates a synthetic counterfactual effectively simulating a parallel universe where an identical county experiences data center deployment under otherwise identical baseline conditions.

We chose a variational autoencoder over a standard autoencoder specifically for its continuous and regularized latent space. This smooth manifold ensures that moving along the "data center vector" in latent space traverses valid, meaningful states rather than unpopulated or unstable gaps.

Our feature set consists of 136 input features alongside the year and data center bin labels. These inputs span structural and geographical measures (one county area, one total population, and two county centroid coordinate features), environmental metrics (20 $\text{PM}_{2.5}$ features), and broad economic indicators (six GDP, six personal income, 14 housing permits, 12 county-wide employment, eight total business establishment, and three neighboring county data center features). Additionally, we included nine establishment, employment, and payroll features across seven distinct industry sectors: industrial, information, primary industries, professional, public services, trade and transport, and unknown. Because many features exhibited extreme skew that standard scaling handled poorly, all input features were transformed using PowerTransformer(method="yeo-johnson"). To prevent exploding reconstruction losses during out-of-sample cross-validation, all scaled values were clipped within $[-10, 10]$.

Directly traversing the continuous latent space along a "data center vector" proved operationally difficult. To overcome this, we adopted a conditional variational autoencoder (CVAE) architecture using two conditioning labels (@fig-cvae). We grouped the log-transformed data center counts into six discrete bins (ranging from 0 to 6). During training, the data center count bin and the sample year were appended to the input feature vector as well as within the latent space. This conditioning allows the network to learn discrete, non-linear economic impacts across different operational scales and years.

![Conditional Variational Autoencoder (CVAE) architecture. The model features a symmetric encoder-decoder structure, each with two hidden layers [128, 16] and [16, 128]. The 136 input features x are conditioned on the Year and DC bin labels at the input layer and again at the 8-dimensional latent vector z before decoding into reconstructed features x′](CVAE_diagram.png){#fig-cvae width=90%}

The encoder compresses inputs through two hidden layers of dimensions [128,16], mirrored symmetrically by the decoder. This rapid compression produced lower reconstruction loss than more gradual compression schedules, indicating substantial redundancy across our input features and supporting the premise that a compact latent space can capture the interaction between data centers and local economies. The bottleneck latent space is set to 8 dimensions; higher-dimensional spaces did not improve performance, while smaller bottlenecks increased reconstruction error. Each hidden layer utilizes ReLU activations and 1D batch normalization. Dropout was tested, but it meaningfully increased the average error, suggesting the compact architecture is not oversized.

The total objective combines Mean Squared Error (MSE) reconstruction loss and Kullback–Leibler (KL) divergence loss. The analytical KL loss regularizes the latent space toward a standard Gaussian prior to enforce continuity, weighted at $\frac{1}{100}$ the magnitude of the reconstruction loss ($\beta = 0.01$). We trained two separate models using the Adam optimizer with gradient clipping to maintain numerical stability: one on Cluster 0 data (25,824 observations) and one on Cluster 1 data (23,248 observations). Models were trained for 50 epochs with a batch size of 1,024 samples, which provided an optimal trade-off between training speed and reconstruction accuracy. Across runs, performance gains occurred primarily between epochs 0 and 10, with diminishing returns thereafter.

```{python}
years = clean_nat_total["year"].astype(int)
ax.set_xticks(years)
ax.set_xticklabels(years, rotation = 45)
ax.set_xlim(2006.80, 2022.20)
ax.margins(x=0)

ymax = clean_nat_total["estabs"].max()
ax.set_ylim(0, ymax * 1.1)

ax.yaxis.set_major_formatter(FuncFormatter(lambda x, pos: f"{int(x):,}"))

ax.grid(axis = "y", alpha = 0.2)
ax.grid(axis = "x", visible = False)

ax.spines["top"].set_visible(False)
ax.spines["right"].set_visible(False)
ax.tick_params(axis = "both", which = "major", labelsize = 12)

fig.tight_layout()

plt.show()
```

One of the main challenges in training the variational autoencoder was defining an appropriate validation strategy. Our first approach was to train the CVAE on historical data and reserve the final two years of our dataset as a temporal test set. However, the model exhibited significantly higher reconstruction error in the final years, which were held out, compared to the training set. This performance gap is likely because the final two years in our time window represent a rapid increase in data center construction (@fig-estabs-over-time) under pandemic-era work from home and increasing demand from the recent popularization of LLMs. The change in business conditions and its resulting boom in data center construction make 2021 and 2022 meaningfully different than the years that came before them. To address this, we transitioned from a temporal split to a spatial holdout strategy using 5-fold group cross-validation (GroupKFold), grouping on county identifiers. This approach trains the model across all years while holding out an entire 20% subset of unique counties in each fold for out-of-sample validation. Rather than forcing the model to forecast future states, this approach reframed the objective toward spatial interpolation across unobserved counties—a theoretical shift that improved reconstruction performance.

Treatment effects were measured by comparing the baseline reconstruction (passing true county data through the full network) against a counterfactual pass where the data center conditioning bin was shifted upward before passing through the decoder. Subtracting baseline output from the counterfactual output yielded the predicted treatment effect across all economic features.
